Area.evidence_source: [/page/1/Text/8] Northern Uganda was severely affected by civil conflict between Uganda Government armed forces and rebel groups (Amone-P'Olak, 2006). This was a period characterized by atrocities and torture in all forms (El-Bushra & Sahl, 2005; Harlacher et al., 2006). As a result two million people were forced to live in IDP camps (Roberts, Ocaka, Browne, Oyok, & Sondrop, 2008). [/page/1/Text/9] People were mainly dependent on humanitarian aid for survival because arable land was inaccessible (Harlacher et al., 2006; Liebling-Kalifani et al., 2008). The conflict led to a breakdown of cultural values (El-Bushra & Sahl, 2005), and people were living in a permanent state of trauma and depression (Ovuga, Oyok & Moro, 2008; Roberts et al., 2008). There were limited opportunities for income, especially for men. As a result they were grossly disempowered and severely restricted in their access to the factors of production i.e., land and cattle, the source of their wealth and power (El-Bushra & Sahl, 2005). Consequently, most men in the camps resorted to excessive consumption of alcohol (Harlacher et al., 2006; Liu Institute for Global Issues, Gulu District NGO Forum & Ker Kwaro Acholi, 2005).
